scenes.text: Memorising is not learning. Even for AI. Imagine a student who memorises last year's exam answers, and then fails when the questions change. [1] AI models can make exactly the same mistake. [2] Let's understand overfitting, and underfitting.

title: Overfitting
vs Underfitting
data.subtitle: Memorising vs understanding
data.hook: Memorising is *not* learning. Even for AI.

scenes.text: Here's the core idea. [1] An overfit model memorises its training data, even the random noise, so it aces practice, but fails on new data. [2] A well fit model learns the real pattern, so it does well on new data too.

left.title: Overfitting
left.label: aces practice, fails the real exam

scenes.text: And there's the opposite problem, underfitting. [1] An underfit model is too simple to learn the pattern at all. [2] It does badly on practice, [3] it does badly on the real test, [4] just like a student who barely studied.

data.definition: When a model is too simple to learn the pattern, so it does badly everywhere.

scenes.text: Here's the whole picture. [1] Practice scores, against real test scores. [2] Underfit, bad on both. [3] Overfit, great on practice, but bad on the real test. [4] And a good fit, good on both, and that's the goal.

So how do you catch overfitting? [1] Compare training accuracy with test accuracy, remember the test set from episode 25? [2] If training is 99 percent, but the test is only 70, it's memorising. [3] If both are close, and high, you've got a good fit.

And how do you fix it? [1] More data, so there's more to learn from, and less to memorise. [2] A simpler model, if it's too big for the task. [3] Regularisation, a gentle penalty for being too complex. [4] And early stopping, ending training before it starts memorising.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think a model that scores 100 percent in training must be amazing. [2] It's often a warning sign. A perfect training score usually means it memorised, so always check it on data it has never seen.

data.myth: A 100% training score means an amazing model.
data.fact: It's often a warning sign of memorising. Always check on data it has never seen.

scenes.text: Quick quiz! A model scores 99 percent in training, but only 60 percent on new data. What's wrong? [1] Pause and think, and if you get it right, comment below! <pause 3.2> [2] Overfitting! It memorised the training data.

data.question: 99% in training, 60% on new data means…

scenes.text: Let's recap. [1] An overfit model memorises, and fails on new data. [2] An underfit model is too simple, and fails everywhere. [3] You spot it by comparing training and test scores.
